lesson.title: Reading the Signs: The Language of Inequality Symbols
lesson.summary: Learn to read and translate the four main inequality symbols, and connect common English phrases like at least and at most to the correct symbol.
lesson.body:
An inequality relies entirely on its symbol to say exactly what kind of comparison is being made, so reading these symbols correctly is just as important as reading the equals sign correctly in an equation. The symbol for less than is written as an angled bracket opening to the right, and greater than is the mirror image, opening to the left. A useful memory trick is that the symbol acts like a hungry mouth that opens toward the larger quantity, so in the statement 3 is less than 7, the open side of the symbol faces the 7. The symbols less than or equal to and greater than or equal to add a small line underneath the angled bracket, and that line is what allows the boundary value itself to count as part of the solution.

Translating English phrases into the correct symbol is where most mistakes happen, because several everyday phrases describe an inequality without using the word less or greater at all. The phrase at least means greater than or equal to, since a requirement of being at least 16 years old allows exactly 16 as well as any older age. The phrase at most, and the phrase no more than, both mean less than or equal to, since a bag that weighs at most 50 pounds is allowed to weigh exactly 50 pounds. The word exceeds means strictly greater than, with no equal case included, and the phrase is under or is below means strictly less than.

Consider two examples of translating a sentence into an inequality using these symbols. A rollercoaster sign states that riders must be at least 48 inches tall to ride. Since at least means greater than or equal to, and h represents a rider's height in inches, the inequality is h is greater than or equal to 48. Notice that a rider who is exactly 48 inches tall is allowed to ride, which matches the everyday meaning of at least. A second example: a shopper decides she can spend at most 50 dollars at the store. Since at most means less than or equal to, and s represents the amount spent, the inequality is s is less than or equal to 50, and spending exactly 50 dollars is allowed under this rule.

Getting these translations backward is a common error worth watching for directly. Writing h is greater than 48, without the or equal to line, would incorrectly exclude a rider who is exactly 48 inches tall from riding, even though the original sign allows that rider on. Reading each phrase carefully, and asking whether the boundary value itself should be included, is the habit that prevents this kind of mistake, and it becomes essential once these symbols are used to graph solutions on a number line and to solve more complex inequalities in the sections ahead.

One more symbol worth mentioning is the not equal to symbol, an equals sign with a single slash through it, which states only that two quantities are different without saying which one is larger. It behaves differently from the other four symbols in this section because it does not describe an ordering at all, only a mismatch, so a solution set built from not equal to typically excludes just one boundary point rather than an entire half of the number line. Keeping the four ordering symbols, less than, greater than, less than or equal to, and greater than or equal to, distinct in memory from this fifth symbol avoids confusion when a problem later asks for all values except one specific number.
